# ARIVA Script: Calculate the Variance of a Sample

**Generated by:** Skill 03 — Script Generation
**Workshop slug:** variance_sample
**Duration:** 10 minutes
**Format:** In-person
**Audience:** Students, no statistics background, 13–30 participants
**ILO:** Calculate the variance of a small dataset by hand, following the three-step process: subtract the mean, square the differences, and average the squared values.

---

## Agenda at a Glance

| Phase | Name | Time | What happens |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Arrival | 0:00–1:00 | Name, topic, ILO stated |
| R | Reactivating | 1:00–2:30 | Show of hands — two classes, same average |
| I | Informing | 2:30–7:00 | Variance intuition + three-step formula with example |
| V | Verarbeitung | 7:00–9:30 | Pairs calculate variance of (2, 4, 4, 4, 6) |
| A | Assessing | 9:30–10:00 | "If variance is 0, what does that mean?" |

---

## Full Script

---

### A — Arrival [0:00–1:00]

**Purpose:** Orient participants. Name, topic, ILO. Nothing else.

> **Script:**
> "Hi, I'm [name]. In the next 10 minutes, we're going to look at **variance** — a way to measure how spread out data is. By the end, you'll be able to **calculate the variance of a small dataset by hand**. Let's go."

> **Cue:** Say the ILO clearly and directly. Don't explain what variance is yet — that's the Informing phase. Don't say "we'll start with some theory" or "today's agenda is…" — you have 60 seconds. Use them.

**Transition:** Move immediately into the first question. No pause.

---

### R — Reactivating [1:00–2:30]

**Purpose:** Connect variance to something everyone has already felt. Read the room — their responses tell you how to pitch the Informing phase.

> **Script:**
> "Quick question before we get into the math. Imagine two classes. Both had an average grade of 70%. In one class, everyone scored between 65 and 75. In the other, grades ranged from 30 to 100. Show of hands — who would rather be in the first class?"
>
> *(Wait for hands. Then:)*
>
> "Who'd rather be in the second?"
>
> *(Take 1–2 quick reasons from volunteers. Listen for words like 'consistent', 'fair', 'risky', 'unpredictable'.)*
>
> "Interesting. Both classes have the same average — but they feel completely different. That difference is what variance captures. Variance is the number that tells you how spread out your data is. Let's see exactly how it works."

> **Cue:** If students are quiet after the hands, prompt: "One word — why'd you pick that one?" Don't let silence stretch past 10 seconds. Move on.

> **Cue:** If a student says "I'd pick the risky class because I could get 100" — great answer. Say: "Exactly — same mean, very different experience. Variance is the tool that captures that difference."

**Transition:** "Here's the concept — and then I'll show you the three steps."

---

### I — Informing [2:30–7:00]

**Purpose:** Build the intuition first, then the formula. One concept, one example. No side trips.

> **Script — Part 1: The intuition [2:30–4:00]**
>
> "Variance measures how far each value in your dataset is from the mean — on average. That's it. If your data is clustered tightly around the mean, variance is low. If it's scattered all over the place, variance is high."
>
> "Think about those two classes again. In the tight class — 65 to 75 — every grade is close to the average of 70. Small distances from the mean. Low variance. In the scattered class — 30 to 100 — some grades are far from 70. Large distances. High variance."

> **Script — Part 2: The three steps [4:00–6:30]**
>
> "How do we calculate it? Three steps."
>
> *(Write on the board as you say each step.)*
>
> "**Step 1: Subtract the mean from each value.**
> This gives you the distance of each value from the mean. Some will be positive, some negative — that's fine.
>
> **Step 2: Square each of those distances.**
> Why? Two reasons. First, squaring makes all the values positive — otherwise the negatives and positives cancel out and you'd always get zero. Second, squaring punishes big deviations more than small ones. A value that's 10 away from the mean contributes 100 to the variance; a value that's 2 away contributes only 4.
>
> **Step 3: Average those squared distances.**
> Add them all up and divide by how many values you have. That average is your variance."

> **Script — worked example [6:30–7:00]**
>
> "Quick example. Scores: 3, 4, 5. Mean is 4."
> *(Write: 3−4=−1, 4−4=0, 5−4=1)*
> "Square them: 1, 0, 1."
> "Average: (1+0+1) ÷ 3 = **0.67**. That's the variance."

> **Cue:** At around 6:00, check in: "Any questions before you try one yourselves?" Take one question only. If someone asks about standard deviation or n−1, say: "Great question — that's the next step after today, we'll get there. For now, let's focus on this."

**Transition:** "Your turn. Find a partner."

---

### V — Verarbeitung [7:00–9:30]

**Purpose:** Participants execute the calculation. Learning happens here, not during Informing.

> **Script:**
> "Here are five numbers: **2, 4, 4, 4, 6**. The mean is 4 — you can trust me on that, or check it quickly. Work in pairs. Calculate the variance. Follow the three steps on the board. Pen and paper only. You have **2 minutes**."
>
> *(Write on board: "2, 4, 4, 4, 6 — mean = 4")*
> *(Start a visible 2-minute timer — phone, projected clock, or call it out.)*
> "Go."

> **Cue:** While they work, walk the room. Listen for confusion at Step 2 (squaring) and Step 3 (dividing by n). Don't correct immediately — let them struggle briefly. Note 1–2 pairs who finish quickly to call on.

> **Cue:** At 1:30: "30 seconds — wrap up your last step."

**To close the task:**
> "Time. What did you get? Shout it out."
> *(Collect answers. You're listening for 1.6. Write a few answers on the board.)*
> "Let's check. Step 1:"
> *(Write: 2−4=−2, 4−4=0, 4−4=0, 4−4=0, 6−4=2)*
> "Step 2, square them: 4, 0, 0, 0, 4."
> "Step 3: (4+0+0+0+4) ÷ 5 = **1.6**. That's the variance."
> "Notice anything? Three of the values are exactly at the mean — they contribute zero to the variance. Only the two outliers drive it."

**Transition:** "Last question."

---

### A — Assessing [9:30–10:00]

**Purpose:** Check whether the ILO landed — not mechanically, but conceptually.

> **Script:**
> "One final question. If I told you the variance of a dataset is exactly **zero** — what does that tell you about the data?"
>
> *(Take 2–3 hands or quick shout-outs.)*
>
> "Exactly — if variance is zero, every value is identical. Nothing is spread from the mean. All the distances are zero. Zero squared is zero. Zero averaged is zero."
>
> "You've just calculated variance. That's it. If you want to go one step further — standard deviation is just the square root of variance, which brings the units back to the original scale. But that's for next time."

> **Cue:** If responses show the concept didn't land (e.g., students say "the data is zero" or give blank looks), don't re-teach. Say: "It means every value in the dataset is the same — there's no variation at all. That's why it's called variance." Then close.

---

## Contingency Notes

**If the group finishes Verarbeitung in under 1 minute:**
> "Fast work. Now tell me: what would happen to the variance if I changed the 2 to a 10? Would it go up or down? Work that out."

**If the group is very slow and time runs out before they finish:**
> Cut the self-check. Walk through Steps 1–3 on the board yourself while they follow along. Then go directly to the Assessing question.

**If someone asks about standard deviation during Informing:**
> "Exactly the right question — standard deviation is the square root of variance, and it brings everything back to the original units. We'll get there. For now, let's finish variance."

**If someone asks why we divide by n and not n−1:**
> "There are actually two versions of this formula — one for a sample, one for a whole population. We're using the simpler one today. It's a great thing to look up after this."
